sources.title: Saprotrophic Capabilities of Neurospora crassa on Charred Plant Biomass
sources.version: Environmental Microbiology 27(6):e70132; version of record published 2025-06-24
sources.locator: Abstract; Experimental Procedures, sections 2.1–2.2; Results on mass loss of wood and grass substrates
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), stated on the article page
sources.scope: Original controlled substrate-decay study; only the named N. crassa strain and tested microcosm substrates are described.
sources.licenseAppliesTo: Article text under CC BY 4.0; no figures or third-party material are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Simpson HJ, Schilling JS (2025). Saprotrophic Capabilities of Neurospora crassa on Charred Plant Biomass. Environmental Microbiology 27(6):e70132. https://doi.org/10.1111/1462-2920.70132. Claims paraphrased.

systematicSearch.scope: Pinned COL26.8 identity verification and bounded reading of one primary study for substrate-decay evidence.
systematicSearch.method: Matched the exact COL usage in the pinned registry and read the primary article's abstract, methods, and reported substrate-decay results. No comprehensive ecology, morphology, life-history, range, fossil, or conservation review was performed.
systematicSearch.inclusionCriteria: Claims explicitly reported from the N. crassa microcosm assays and their tested substrates.
systematicSearch.exclusionCriteria: Prior literature cited by the article, untested field mechanisms, whole-species physiological generalization, and unassessed facets.

gaps: The cited study does not provide a species-level morphological assessment.
The microcosm study does not assess reproduction or a complete developmental life history.

claims.text: In controlled assays, N. crassa did not show enhanced decay of pyrolyzed wood or grass relative to the tested non-fire-associated fungi; it degraded untreated grass substrates by more than 20% mass loss but struggled to degrade wood, with less than 6% mass loss. These are results for the tested strain and lab microcosms, not measurements of its field performance after fires.
claims.locator: Abstract; Results, decay mass loss for wood and grass substrates; Experimental Procedures, single-strain microcosm design
claims.placeTimeScope: Laboratory microcosm assays using untreated and pyrolyzed substrates, including 225°C and 350°C heat treatments; the claim is limited to the study's experimental conditions.
claims.lifeStatus: A controlled cultured strain was assessed; the study does not characterize wild population abundance, seasonal activity, or field colonization.

gaps: The article tests substrate decay in controlled microcosms; natural post-fire colonization, population dynamics, broader substrate use, and interactions in field communities remain unassessed.
No species-level evolutionary or population-genomic analysis is used for this dossier.
The experiment is not a georeferenced distribution survey.
No fossil or paleontological search was performed.
No formal conservation assessment or population-trend review was performed.

reasons: Only one bounded substrate-decay result from a controlled primary study has been assessed; morphology, life history, evolution, distribution, fossil, and conservation facets remain not-assessed.
No systematic literature search or complete comparison with the COL26.8 species concept has been completed.
No independent expert review has been completed.

sources.title: Population genomics of Fusarium graminearum reveals signatures of divergent evolution within a major cereal pathogen
sources.version: PLOS ONE 13(3):e0194616; version of record published 2018-03-27
sources.locator: Abstract; Results, Population genomic structure; Figure 1; Materials and Methods, Genome sequencing
sources.license: Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal public domain dedication, stated on the article page
sources.scope: Original whole-genome population study of three North American F. graminearum cereal-crop isolate groups; dossier statements are limited to the sampled isolates.
sources.rightsHolder: Amy C. Kelly and Todd J. Ward; article released under CC0 1.0
sources.licenseAppliesTo: Article and its text under CC0 1.0; separately credited material may carry separate terms. No figures are reproduced.
sources.attribution: Kelly AC, Ward TJ (2018). PLOS ONE 13(3):e0194616. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0194616. Claims paraphrased.

systematicSearch.scope: Pinned COL26.8 identity verification and bounded reading of one primary whole-genome population study.
systematicSearch.method: Matched the exact COL usage in the pinned registry and read the article abstract, population-genomics results, Figure 1 description, and sample collection methods. No comprehensive global distribution, ecological, fossil, or conservation review was performed.
systematicSearch.inclusionCriteria: Claims directly reported for the paper's North American cereal-crop isolates and genome analyses.
systematicSearch.exclusionCriteria: Secondary-source range statements, inference beyond the sampled groups, claims from other Fusarium species, and unassessed facets.

gaps: The cited genomic study does not provide a species-level morphological assessment.
The cited study does not directly assess the complete reproductive or developmental life history.

claims.text: The study's population-genomic panel comprised 60 F. graminearum isolates collected from cereal crops in the northern United States and southern Canada: 20 NA1/15ADON, 20 NA2/3ADON, and 20 NX-2 isolates. This describes the source and structure of that sample, not their prevalence across the species' range or all host plants.
claims.locator: Abstract; Materials and Methods, Genome sequencing; Figure 1
claims.placeTimeScope: North American cereal-crop isolates selected for the 2018 population-genomic analysis; exact dates and exhaustive site coverage are not claimed here.
claims.lifeStatus: Crop-associated field isolates; the study does not resolve wild-host populations or fungal domestication.

gaps: This selected population-genomic panel is not a comprehensive host, habitat, or geographic survey; the broader ecological niches and field prevalence remain unassessed.

claims.text: Bayesian clustering and phylogenomic analyses of the 60 sampled isolates supported three North American populations (NA1, NA2, and NA3); eight NX-2 isolates had admixed ancestry across the groups. This is population structure in the study panel, not a species-wide phylogeny or global evolutionary history.
claims.locator: Abstract; Results, Population genomic structure; Figure 1 and its legend
claims.placeTimeScope: Whole-genome data from 60 cereal-crop isolates sampled across North America; group assignments follow the authors' 2018 analyses.
claims.lifeStatus: Molecular evidence from archived crop-associated isolates; no current population status is inferred.

gaps: The study is geographically limited and does not establish a global species phylogeny, divergence dates, or the present distribution of each population.
The study samples selected North American isolates and does not establish a complete native, introduced, or global range.
No fossil or paleontological search was performed.
No formal conservation assessment or population-trend review was performed.

reasons: Only study-bounded crop-isolate sampling and population-genomic evidence from one primary study have been assessed; morphology, life history, distribution, fossil, and conservation facets remain not-assessed.
No systematic literature search or complete comparison with the COL26.8 species concept has been completed.
No independent expert review has been completed.
